prompt: A colleague runs `aws s3 mb s3://quitanda-test` in a terminal where `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL` is not set and the keys are `test`. What happens?

choices.text: moto creates the bucket, as it does with the variable set
choices.why: Without the variable the request never reaches moto.

choices.text: The real AWS refuses the key, and nothing is created
choices.why: Right: `InvalidAccessKeyId`.

choices.text: The command line refuses to run without an endpoint
choices.why: It has a default endpoint: Amazon's.

choices.text: A bucket is created in a real account and billed
choices.why: Only if the terminal held real credentials, which `test` is not.

prompt: A Glue job started in moto ends in `SUCCEEDED`. What may you conclude about the same job on AWS?
hint: What does moto do with code it is asked to run?

choices.text: That it will succeed, since the request is identical
choices.why: moto runs no Spark; the success says nothing about the script.

choices.text: That the request was well formed, and nothing about the job itself
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: That it will succeed if the IAM role exists
choices.why: Neither the role nor the script was evaluated.

choices.text: That it ran faster than it will on AWS
choices.why: It did not run at all.

prompt: A bucket holds `raw/orders/a.csv` and `raw/payments/b.csv` and nothing else. How many objects are in it?

choices.text: Two
choices.why: Right; `raw/`, `raw/orders/` and `raw/payments/` are prefixes.

choices.text: Five: two files and three folders
choices.why: Folders are drawn from prefixes and are not objects.

choices.text: Three: two files and the folder `raw/`
choices.why: No object has the key `raw/`.

choices.text: Four: each file and its parent folder
choices.why: Parent folders exist only in listings.

prompt: Which of these make a bad bucket name, by AWS's rules or by this course's scheme? Choose all that apply.
hint: Lowercase, no dots, no people, company-layer-environment.

choices.text: `quitanda-curated-prod`
choices.why: It follows the scheme.

choices.text: `Quitanda-Curated`
choices.why: Capitals are refused.

choices.text: `quitanda.logs.prod`
choices.why: Legal, and it breaks HTTPS to the usual address.

choices.text: `quitanda-ana-raw`
choices.why: A person's name; people move and the bucket stays.

prompt: S3 Standard in sa-east-1 costs 0.0405 USD per GB-month. What do 2,000 GB cost for one month, in whole USD?

Quitanda puts 2,500 GB in Glacier Deep Archive (0.00320 USD per GB-month, 180 days minimum) and deletes all of it after 60 days. Counting a month as 30 days, what does the storage cost in total, in whole USD?

One terabyte is read back in full twelve times a year. By the lesson's yearly table (Standard 497.66; Standard-IA 271.56 plus 10.24 a read; Glacier Instant Retrieval 101.99 plus 30.72 a read), which class is cheapest for it?

choices.text: Standard, since a monthly read is frequent access
choices.why: Standard costs 497.66; Standard-IA with twelve reads is 271.56 + 122.88 = 394.44.

choices.text: Standard-IA
choices.why: Right: 394.44, against 470.63 for Instant Retrieval and 497.66 for Standard.

choices.text: Glacier Instant Retrieval, whose storage line is the lowest of the three
choices.why: 101.99 + 12 × 30.72 = 470.63: the reads eat the saving.

choices.text: Deep Archive, read back in bulk every month
choices.why: Cheap in money, and every read waits up to 48 hours for a restore; a monthly report cannot.

prompt: A job restores an object from Glacier Flexible Retrieval with the Standard tier and reads it with `get-object` on the next line. Against moto the read succeeds. What does the same job meet on AWS?

choices.text: The same success, because the restore request was accepted
choices.why: Accepted is not finished. moto finishes a restore at once; S3 takes hours.

choices.text: `InvalidObjectState` on the read, for three to five hours
choices.why: Right: until the copy is ready, `ongoing-request` is `"true"` and every `GET` is refused.

choices.text: A refusal of the restore itself, as the tier is reserved for Deep Archive
choices.why: Standard is a tier of both archive classes; the one missing from Deep Archive is Expedited.

choices.text: A slow read that streams the bytes as the archive finds them
choices.why: There is no slow read of an archived object, only no read until the restore ends.

prompt: Order these restores by how soon AWS documents the readable copy as ready, soonest first.

A pipeline user may `s3:DeleteObject` and is denied `s3:DeleteObjectVersion`. A bug makes it run `aws s3 rm --recursive` over `raw/` in a versioned bucket. What is the state of `raw/` afterwards, and the way back?

choices.text: Every key has a delete marker on top and every version underneath; deleting the markers brings the keys back
choices.why: Right: a delete with no version only adds a marker, and the user could not have destroyed a version.

choices.text: The objects are gone, and only a backup restores them
choices.why: That is an unversioned bucket. Here nothing was removed.

choices.text: The command was refused, as the user lacks `DeleteObjectVersion`
choices.why: `aws s3 rm` sends no version id, so it needs only `DeleteObject`, which the user has.

choices.text: The current versions are destroyed and the older ones stay
choices.why: Destroying a version takes a delete that names it, which this user cannot send.

prompt: A 50 GB table is rewritten every night in a versioned bucket, and the only rule is `NoncurrentVersionExpiration` with `NoncurrentDays` 14. Once the bucket has settled, how many GB does it hold for this table, in whole GB?
hint: Lesson 3. Count the current version as well.

prompt: A version is locked in compliance mode until October 2027. Which of these requests does S3 accept for it before that date?

choices.text: Moving the retain-until date later, to 2028
choices.why: Right: a compliance retention can be extended and never shortened.

choices.text: Switching the mode to governance, keeping the date
choices.why: The mode of a compliance retention cannot be changed; moto allowed it and S3 does not.

choices.text: A delete naming the version, sent by the root user
choices.why: No permission, the root user's included, deletes it before its date.

choices.text: A delete naming the version with `--bypass-governance-retention`
choices.why: The bypass is for governance mode; compliance has none.

prompt: Quitanda's click bucket holds tens of millions of 10 KB objects. A rule created this year moves them to Standard-IA after 30 days, and two months later the storage bill has not dropped. What is the likeliest reason?

choices.text: Standard-IA costs the same as Standard per GB-month
choices.why: It costs 0.02210 against 0.04050; the price is not the reason.

choices.text: Life-cycle rules wait a year before their first run
choices.why: S3 evaluates rules about once a day.

choices.text: The rule was refused, since 30 days is below the minimum
choices.why: 30 days is exactly the minimum S3 asks for a transition to Standard-IA.

choices.text: Objects under 128 KB are not transitioned by default
choices.why: Right: `all_storage_classes_128K` leaves them in Standard, where a 10 KB object is not billed as 128 KB.

prompt: A Lambda function, running under a role whose session lasts one hour, presigns a supplier's invoice with `--expires-in 604800`. The supplier opens the link the next day. What does S3 answer?

choices.text: The invoice, as seven days have not passed
choices.why: A URL signed with temporary credentials dies with them, whatever `X-Amz-Expires` says.

choices.text: `403`, because the credentials that signed it have expired
choices.why: Right: the session ended after an hour, and the URL with it.

choices.text: Nothing: the command line refuses to sign past the session
choices.why: Signing checks nothing; the limit is S3's, at the moment of use.

choices.text: `404`, as a URL for a role is stored only for an hour
choices.why: No URL is stored anywhere; S3 recomputes the signature when it is used.

prompt: Block Public Access is on at the account level, all four switches. A developer wants the shop's product images public and applies a policy allowing `"Principal": "*"` to `s3:GetObject` on `quitanda-site-prod/images/*` only. What does AWS do?

choices.text: Accepts it, because the resource is narrowed to one prefix
choices.why: A narrow public grant is still a public grant, and the switches refuse every one.

choices.text: Accepts it, and refuses anonymous reads under it
choices.why: That is `RestrictPublicBuckets` alone; `BlockPublicPolicy` stops the policy before it is stored.

choices.text: Refuses the policy with `AccessDenied`
choices.why: Right: `BlockPublicPolicy` at the account level refuses any policy that grants public access, in every bucket.

choices.text: Accepts it once the bucket's own switches are turned off
choices.why: The stricter of the two levels wins, and the account's stays on.

prompt: The logs bucket gets a policy that denies `s3:*` to any principal whose `aws:PrincipalOrgID` is not Quitanda's. People read it as before, and the next morning a log delivery that writes into it has stopped. What did the policy forget?

choices.text: An exception for services, via `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`
choices.why: Right: a service acting for you is not a principal of your organisation.

choices.text: An `Allow` for the log delivery, which outranks the `Deny`
choices.why: An explicit deny wins over every allow; the fix has to be in the deny's condition.

choices.text: The `aws:SecureTransport` condition, as services send plain HTTP
choices.why: Nothing here is about TLS; the delivery was refused for not being in the organisation.

choices.text: The bucket ARN without `/*`, which delivery uses
choices.why: The resources are not the problem: the principal is.

prompt: A reporting role's policy allows `s3:GetObject` and `s3:ListBucket`, both with `"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::quitanda-curated-prod/*"`. On AWS, what can the role do?

choices.text: Read objects and list the bucket
choices.why: Listing is an action on the bucket, whose ARN has no `/*`.

choices.text: Read objects, and not list the bucket
choices.why: Right: the `/*` resource names objects, so `ListBucket` matches nothing.

choices.text: Neither, as one resource cannot serve two actions
choices.why: One statement can list several actions; each is matched against the resources.

choices.text: List the bucket and read nothing until `s3:*` is added
choices.why: It is the reverse: the objects match and the bucket does not.

prompt: In one month Quitanda sends 10,240 GB to the internet (0.15000 USD per GB for the first 10,240) and copies 1,000 GB to us-east-1 (0.13800 USD per GB). What is the transfer bill, in whole USD?
Which of these movements of bytes, in sa-east-1, put a per-GB charge on Quitanda's bill? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A machine in one zone reading the lake bucket in the same region
choices.why: S3 is regional: reading it from any zone of the region costs no transfer, only requests.

choices.text: A database replicating to its standby in another zone
choices.why: Between zones, 0.01000 a GB, each direction.

choices.text: A private subnet reading S3 through a NAT gateway
choices.why: The NAT gateway charges for every GB it processes, even to S3 next door.

choices.text: The bucket sending objects to CloudFront
choices.why: S3 to CloudFront is 0.00000; CloudFront then bills its own delivery.

choices.text: A supplier uploading files into the raw bucket from the internet
choices.why: Data coming in is free; only the `PUT` requests are billed.

prompt: Quitanda turns requester pays on for the bucket a partner copies every night. The partner's job, unchanged and still allowed by the bucket policy, now fails with `403`. What is the likeliest cause?

choices.text: Its requests do not say they accept the charge
choices.why: Right: without `x-amz-request-payer: requester` (`--request-payer requester`), S3 refuses.

choices.text: Requester pays refuses every account but the owner
choices.why: It exists for other accounts; it refuses only anonymous requests and ones that do not accept the charge.

choices.text: The partner's account must first pay for the storage too
choices.why: The owner keeps paying for storage; the requester pays requests and transfer.

choices.text: The bucket must be public for another account to pay
choices.why: The opposite: a requester-pays bucket refuses anonymous requests outright.

prompt: An app writes one 2 KB object per order, ten million a month, and a report reads all of them every morning. Which change takes the most off the S3 bill?

choices.text: Moving the objects to Standard-IA after 30 days
choices.why: Storage is the smallest meter here, a 2 KB object is billed as 128 KB in IA, and its `GET` costs more.

choices.text: Fewer, larger files holding many orders each
choices.why: Right: the bill is requests, priced per object; the same bytes in large files cost fractions of a cent to read.

choices.text: Compressing each object to half its size
choices.why: A request costs the same whatever its size, and the count of objects does not change.

choices.text: Listing the prefix first, so only new objects are read
choices.why: A `LIST` is billed like a `PUT`, and the report still reads every object.

prompt: An RDS PostgreSQL instance was created Single-AZ with 1,000 GiB of gp3 (0.219 USD per GB-month), and the database inside it holds 120 GiB. What does its storage cost in a month, in whole USD?
The orders instance has sat at 95% CPU since a new report shipped on Monday. Somebody proposes moving it to a class four times larger. What does the lesson make of that?

choices.text: It is RDS's job to scale it, so the request goes to AWS support
choices.why: RDS reports the CPU; it does not decide your class, and it does not read your queries.

choices.text: It is the expensive way to hide what is probably a query or a missing index
choices.why: Right: queries and indexes stay yours after the move, and a bigger class is one command.

choices.text: It is right, as managed engines tune queries themselves
choices.why: Nothing inside the engine moved to AWS: the slow query is still Quitanda's.

choices.text: It cannot work, since a class is fixed when the instance is made
choices.why: Changing class is one `modify-db-instance` and a restart.

prompt: In moto, an instance created with `--engine sqlserver-se` came back with `LicenseModel` `general-public-license`. What is true of the same instance on AWS?

choices.text: It is free of licence too, as RDS ships open engines
choices.why: SQL Server is Microsoft's and is never open source.

choices.text: The licence is in its hourly price
choices.why: Right: 1.087 an hour against 0.221 for the same size of machine; moto fills the field without reasoning.

choices.text: It needs a licence of your own from Microsoft, brought to AWS
choices.why: That is Oracle Enterprise and Db2; SQL Server on RDS is licence included.

choices.text: It is refused unless `--license-model` is named
choices.why: SQL Server has one model on RDS, and it is the default.

prompt: On a real PostgreSQL, the `context` column of `pg_settings` reads `___` for a setting such as `max_connections`, read only when the server starts.
After a Multi-AZ failover that AWS reports as finished in under two minutes, Quitanda's Python workers are back and its Java service still times out twenty minutes later. What is the likeliest cause?

choices.text: The standby lost the transactions committed just before the failure
choices.why: The standby is synchronous: it holds every committed transaction. And losing data would not cause timeouts.

choices.text: The endpoint changed, and the Java service still has the old name configured
choices.why: The name does not change in a failover; what is behind it does.

choices.text: The Java runtime cached the old address of the name and keeps knocking at it
choices.why: Right: the JVM's default DNS cache can last forever, and AWS recommends under a minute.

choices.text: The new standby is still being built, and the primary waits for it
choices.why: The promoted standby serves while the new one is built in the other zone.

prompt: The orders database is 3,000 GB and writes 1,000 GB of write-ahead log a month. A read replica of it runs in us-east-1, and transfer to us-east-1 is 0.138 USD per GB. What does the replication traffic cost in a month, in whole USD?
Quitanda's SQL Server finance database needs a standby, and an engineer proposes a Multi-AZ DB cluster because it fails over faster. What is wrong with the proposal?

choices.text: The cluster is offered for PostgreSQL and MySQL only
choices.why: Right: SQL Server's standby is the Multi-AZ instance, 60 to 120 seconds.

choices.text: A cluster fails over more slowly than an instance does
choices.why: It is faster, under 35 seconds by AWS's documentation.

choices.text: Its readers cannot answer queries until a failover happens
choices.why: That describes the Multi-AZ instance's standby; the cluster's readers serve reads.

choices.text: Nothing: moto created the cluster, so AWS will too
choices.why: moto created a cluster with no instances at all; its acceptance proves nothing.

prompt: São Paulo's primary is lost with no standby, and Quitanda promotes its read replica in us-east-1. What should the team expect to find in the promoted instance?

choices.text: Every committed transaction, as replication is synchronous
choices.why: A replica hears of a write after the commit; that is Multi-AZ's property, not a replica's.

choices.text: The database up to the last daily snapshot
choices.why: A replica replays the log continuously; it is not rebuilt from snapshots.

choices.text: Everything but the last moments of replica lag
choices.why: Right: replication is asynchronous, so promotion accepts losing what had not arrived.

choices.text: An empty database, since promotion cuts the link
choices.why: Promotion cuts the link and keeps the data the replica had.

prompt: An Aurora cluster has one `db.r7g.large` and a 1,000 GB volume. I/O-Optimized adds 96.34 USD a month for the instance and 0.238 USD per GB-month for storage; Standard charges 0.28 USD per million I/Os. Above how many million I/Os a month is I/O-Optimized cheaper? Answer in whole millions.
An Aurora cluster has a writer, two replicas and a volume holding 500 GB. How much storage does the bill charge for?

choices.text: 1,500 GB, one copy per instance
choices.why: Replicas read the same volume and keep no copy of the data.

choices.text: 3,000 GB, for the six copies of every segment
choices.why: The six copies are AWS's cost and not a line on the bill.

choices.text: 500 GB, once
choices.why: Right: one shared volume, billed by what it holds, however many instances read it.

choices.text: Whatever size was allocated when the cluster was made
choices.why: An Aurora volume has no size to choose; it grows with the data.

prompt: A cluster has a provisioned writer and a Serverless v2 reader in promotion tier 5, which sits at its minimum most of the day. The writer fails at the evening peak and the reader is promoted. What is the risk?

choices.text: None, since a promotion copies the writer's capacity across
choices.why: Only a reader in tier 0 or 1 is kept at the writer's capacity.

choices.text: It takes the writes while still small, and lags until it scales
choices.why: Right: in tiers 2 to 15 a serverless reader scales on its own load, so it is small when the load has been low.

choices.text: It is missing the writes it did not replay in time
choices.why: An Aurora replica reads the same volume; no data is missing.

choices.text: It cannot be promoted at all, as a serverless instance never writes
choices.why: A serverless instance can be a writer; the dev cluster of the lesson has one.

prompt: Quitanda's heavy morning reports, sent to the reader endpoint, slow down the shop's pages that read from the same replicas. Which change fits what the lesson describes?

choices.text: Point the reports at the cluster endpoint, so they run on the writer
choices.why: That moves the load onto the instance taking every checkout.

choices.text: Point the reports at one replica's own instance endpoint
choices.why: An instance endpoint is for diagnosing a machine, and breaks when that machine changes role.

choices.text: Add a larger replica and name it alone in a custom endpoint for the reports
choices.why: Right: a custom endpoint keeps a group of replicas apart for one job.

choices.text: Switch the cluster to I/O-Optimized, so heavy reads are free
choices.why: That changes the bill, not who competes for the same replica.

prompt: A colleague proposes order sort keys of the form `ORDER#o-10002#2026-10-05`, id before date, "so that ids are easy to find". Which of Quitanda's access patterns does that break?

choices.text: A customer's profile, read by `get-item`
choices.why: The profile's key is `PROFILE` and does not change.

choices.text: A customer's orders between two dates
choices.why: Right: the collection would sort by id, and a `BETWEEN` on dates needs the date first.

choices.text: One order with its lines, read by its prefix
choices.why: The lines would still extend the order's key and sort under it.

choices.text: None, since the sort key can be queried by any part of it
choices.why: A sort-key condition is a contiguous run from the start of the string, never a `contains`.

prompt: Two back-office screens read the same profile at `version` 3. Each saves with the condition `version = :seen` (3) and the update `version = version + 1`. What happens to the second save?

choices.text: It overwrites the first, as the last write always wins
choices.why: That is the plain put; the condition exists to stop it.

choices.text: It succeeds and sets `version` to 5
choices.why: The item is at 4 now, so `version = 3` is false.

choices.text: Refused with `ConditionalCheckFailedException`
choices.why: Right: the first save moved the version, so the second's condition is false and nothing is written.

choices.text: It is merged with the first, attribute by attribute
choices.why: DynamoDB never merges two writes; a write happens whole or not at all.

prompt: Order these sort keys of one item collection as DynamoDB keeps them, first to last.

The finance team wants new questions every week: revenue per district, per product, per hour, compared with last year. What does writing their access patterns down say about serving them from the DynamoDB table?

choices.text: That one more sort-key prefix per question will do
choices.why: A key is built for a pattern known in advance; a new one each week means rewriting items each week.

choices.text: That a scan with a filter is cheap enough for weekly use
choices.why: A filter saves nothing; every scan reads the whole table.

choices.text: That they belong in a warehouse or the lake, fed from the table
choices.why: Right: ad hoc aggregates across everything are what a store read by key fights.

choices.text: That DynamoDB will plan the aggregates if the table is large enough
choices.why: DynamoDB has no query planner at any size.

prompt: An eventually consistent scan with a filter reads 40 MB of items (40 × 1,048,576 bytes) and returns 1 MB of them. A read unit covers 4 KB (4,096 bytes), and an eventually consistent read costs half a unit per block. How many read units does AWS charge for it?
The index `pending` projects `KEYS_ONLY`. The dispatch screen now wants each open order's `total_cents` beside its key. What does a query on the index return?

choices.text: The keys and the totals, fetched from the table on the way
choices.why: That is what a local index can do; a global index returns only what was projected.

choices.text: An error, because `total_cents` is not in the index
choices.why: Asking for an attribute that is absent is not an error; it just does not come back.

choices.text: Keys only: the totals were never projected
choices.why: Right: a global index cannot reach back into the table, so the projection is decided by what the question needs.

choices.text: Whole items, since keys-only covers every attribute of a key
choices.why: `KEYS_ONLY` copies the index's keys and the table's, and nothing else.

prompt: An app sends a customer's browser the raw `LastEvaluatedKey` of their order list, and takes it back as the start of the next page. What is the risk the lesson points to?

choices.text: The key can expire after a minute, and the next page fails
choices.why: A position does not expire; it is just a key.

choices.text: A client can send back a key for another customer
choices.why: Right: encode it or keep it on the server, and check the next request is still for that user's partition.

choices.text: The browser cannot hold a key larger than 1 MB
choices.why: The key is a few bytes; 1 MB is the size of a page of data.

choices.text: Nothing: a `LastEvaluatedKey` holds no table data
choices.why: It is the table's key, and here the key names a customer.

prompt: moto showed a new global index `ACTIVE` at once. On AWS, while it backfills from the items already in the table, it reports the status `___` and refuses queries.
An `update-item` grows an item from 3,000 bytes to 5,000 bytes. A write unit covers 1 KB (1,024 bytes). How many write units does AWS charge for the update?
hint: Lesson 11. An update is charged on one of the two sizes.

prompt: A table provisioned at 10,000 write units gets an index keyed on `status`, and every new order is written with `status = PENDING`. At 2,000 new orders a second, writes are throttled while the table's metrics show it mostly idle. Why?

choices.text: Burst capacity was spent and is refilled only at midnight
choices.why: Burst is up to five minutes of unused capacity, kept continuously, and the table has plenty unused.

choices.text: One index key takes every write, past one partition's limit
choices.why: Right: a hot partition, which no table setting lifts; sharding the key spreads it.

choices.text: The index needs its own 10,000 units before it accepts writes
choices.why: More index capacity does not lift the ceiling of one key on one partition.

choices.text: Throttling only starts once adaptive capacity is turned off
choices.why: Adaptive capacity is always there, and it cannot lift one key past the partition's limit.

prompt: A provisioned table with target-tracking autoscaling is throttled for the first minutes of every 18:00 promotion, then recovers. The promotion's time is known a week ahead. Which change fits the lesson?

choices.text: Lower the target from 70% to 40%, so it scales out sooner
choices.why: Any target still reacts to load that has already arrived, minutes late, and costs more all day.

choices.text: Scheduled scaling, raised shortly before 18:00
choices.why: Right: a spike at a known time is met by scheduled scaling, before it arrives.

choices.text: Shorten `ScaleInCooldown` to zero
choices.why: Scale-in is the way down; the problem is going up late.

choices.text: Nothing: the throttled writes are lost and the next ones succeed
choices.why: The SDK retries them, and the customer waits; that is the cost to remove.

prompt: An on-demand table has never seen more than 2,000 writes a second. A campaign sends it 5,000 a second within a few minutes. By AWS's documented behaviour, what happens?

choices.text: Every write is served, as on demand has no ceiling
choices.why: On demand takes up to double its previous peak at once, not any rate at all.

choices.text: Writes past about 4,000 a second are throttled
choices.why: Right: traffic more than doubling the previous peak within about half an hour is throttled while the table grows.

choices.text: The table switches itself to provisioned to cope
choices.why: A mode switch is only ever an `update-table` somebody sends.

choices.text: moto's load test showed 363 writes a second, so it holds
choices.why: moto never throttles; a load test there measures the program and the laptop.

prompt: The consumer that feeds Quitanda's product search from the table's DynamoDB stream was broken for three days before anybody noticed. It is fixed now. What brings the search index back in line?

choices.text: Restarting it from `TRIM_HORIZON`, which holds every change since it stopped
choices.why: `TRIM_HORIZON` is the oldest record still kept, and records older than 24 hours are gone.

choices.text: Rebuild it from a full read of the table, then follow on
choices.why: Right: two days of changes left the stream for good, and only the table still has their result.

choices.text: Disabling and enabling the stream, which replays the table into it
choices.why: A new stream starts empty; changes made before it existed are not in it.

choices.text: Nothing: DynamoDB keeps unread records until a reader takes them
choices.why: A stream is not a queue; a record goes a day after it was written, read or not.

prompt: A Lambda function on a stream receives batches of 100, and record 61 of one batch makes it fail every time. With the mapping's default settings, what happens on AWS?

choices.text: Lambda skips record 61 and carries on with record 62
choices.why: By default nothing is skipped: the whole batch is retried.

choices.text: The batch is retried whole and the shard waits
choices.why: Right: the next batch must not overtake this one, so the shard is blocked; `--maximum-retry-attempts` and `--bisect-batch-on-function-error` limit that.

choices.text: The 60 records already applied are rolled back by Lambda
choices.why: Lambda undoes nothing; they are delivered again, and a naive function applies them twice.

choices.text: The stream marks the record as poisoned and removes it
choices.why: The stream never removes a record before its 24 hours.

prompt: A reader of your own polls 5 shards of a DynamoDB stream once a second each, for a 30-day month. Ignoring the free allowance, at 0.30 USD per million `GetRecords` calls, what does it cost, to the nearest whole USD?

pairs.left: a running total of `total_cents` per customer

a job that only needs to know which keys changed

prompt: To spare the database, a developer makes the checkout read the stock count from the cache, where the product page already shows "3 left". What does the lesson make of that?

choices.text: Fine, as long as every key carries a time to live
choices.why: A TTL bounds how stale the copy is; it does not make a stale copy safe to sell from.

choices.text: Wrong: the sale's decrement belongs to the database
choices.why: Right: never let a cached copy decide something that costs money.

choices.text: Fine on Valkey, which replicates writes synchronously
choices.why: Replication is asynchronous, and staleness is about the database, not the replicas.

choices.text: Wrong only under `allkeys-lru`, which may evict the count
choices.why: Eviction is one problem; a correct but old count is the other, under any policy.

prompt: At 03:00 a job warms the cache with the 1,000 busiest product pages, each written with `EX 300`. Every night at 03:05 the database spikes. What change does the lesson suggest?

choices.text: Write the keys with no time to live, so they never expire together
choices.why: Keys with no TTL fill the cache with things nobody reads, and on the default policy writes start failing.

choices.text: Raise every TTL to 3,600 seconds
choices.why: They would still expire in the same second, an hour later.

choices.text: Switch the eviction policy to `noeviction`
choices.why: Eviction is about a full cache; these keys are expiring, not being evicted.

choices.text: Give each key 300 seconds plus a random few
choices.why: Right: spreading the expiries keeps a thousand misses from landing in one second.

prompt: Quitanda moves its cache to a replication group with cluster mode enabled. A command that reads `cart:c-17` and `profile:c-17` together, which worked before, now fails. Why?

choices.text: The two keys sit in different hash slots
choices.why: Right: that is the price of splitting 16,384 slots across shards.

choices.text: Cluster mode stores strings only, like Memcached
choices.why: Cluster mode keeps every data type; it changes where keys live.

choices.text: Reads must now go to the reader endpoint
choices.why: The client computes the owning shard; the failure is about the two keys, not the endpoint.

choices.text: The replica has not received the cart yet
choices.why: Lag would return old data, not refuse the command.

prompt: Match each eviction policy to what a full cache does under it.

pairs.right: evicts only keys that have a time to live
evicts any key, least recently used first

right_distractors: writes the oldest keys to disk

prompt: A nightly report joins the warehouse with history in the lake through Redshift Spectrum, scanning 0.6 TB of files each run. At 5.00 USD per TB scanned, what does it cost in a 30-day month, in whole USD?
A `deliveries` table gets `COMPOUND SORTKEY (store_id, dt)`, and nearly every report on it asks for one week across all forty stores. How well do the zone maps serve those reports?

choices.text: Badly: most blocks are read
choices.why: Right: a compound key serves its first column; the date should lead when reports filter by date.

choices.text: As well as `(dt, store_id)`, since both columns are in the key
choices.why: That is what an interleaved key would aim at; a compound key weighs its columns in order.

choices.text: Perfectly, because zone maps index every column separately
choices.why: Every column has zone maps, and they only skip blocks when the rows are sorted by that column.

choices.text: Not at all, as zone maps work only for the distribution key
choices.why: Distribution decides the slice; zone maps follow the sort order.

prompt: The support screen shows one order by its id, thousands of times an hour, and somebody proposes serving it from the Redshift warehouse, which already holds every order. What is wrong with that?

choices.text: Redshift cannot filter on a column that is not the sort key
choices.why: It can filter on any column; it just reads blocks to do it.

choices.text: One row by key is what Redshift does worst
choices.why: Right: Redshift is built to read millions of rows and add them up, not to answer by key.

choices.text: The warehouse holds orders only after a nightly delay of a week
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says that; the load is nightly.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the leader node has enough memory
choices.why: The leader plans and gathers; the shape of the question is the problem.

prompt: In Redshift Serverless, the team deletes the workgroup `quitanda-adhoc` and creates a new one with a different base capacity, attached to the same namespace. What happens to the tables?

choices.text: They are deleted with the workgroup, as compute and storage go together
choices.why: They are kept apart so that one can change without the other.

choices.text: They are copied to the new workgroup, which takes as long as the data is large
choices.why: Nothing is copied: the data never lived in the workgroup.

choices.text: Untouched: the data was never the workgroup's
choices.why: Right: the workgroup is what the warehouse runs on, the namespace what it is.

choices.text: They become read-only until the base capacity matches the old one
choices.why: The capacity is free to change; that is a reason for the split.

prompt: Athena bills the bytes read rounded up to a whole MB, with 10 MB as the least for any query, and nothing for a query that fails. Three queries read 2 MB, 15.2 MB, and nothing at all because the third failed. How many MB are billed in all?

`orders` uses partition projection with `storage.location.template` `s3://quitanda-curated-prod/orders/dt=${dt}/`. A fix-up job writes 15 October's corrected file under `orders/date=2026-10-15/`. What do queries for that day see?

choices.text: The corrected file, since projection needs nothing registered
choices.why: Projection computes keys from the template, and this key is not one of them.

choices.text: Both files, the old and the corrected one
choices.why: Only the prefix the template produces is listed.

choices.text: Whatever is under `dt=2026-10-15/`; the new file is invisible
choices.why: Right: the template is a promise about the keys, and a file under any other name is not read.

choices.text: An error, until `MSCK REPAIR TABLE` adds the new prefix
choices.why: With projection on, the catalog's list of partitions is not what is read.

prompt: The CSV table is partitioned by `dt`, and each file also has an `order_date` column with the same date. A dashboard asks `... WHERE order_date = '2026-10-15'` every hour. What does each query read?

choices.text: One day's file, because the two columns hold the same values
choices.why: The engine cannot know they agree; only the key column is settled before reading.

choices.text: Only the `order_date` column of every file
choices.why: A CSV has no way to say where a column starts; lines are read whole.

choices.text: Nothing, as a filter is applied before the scan
choices.why: A filter on a column inside the files is applied to what was read.

choices.text: Every file of every day, whole; filtering on `dt` would open one
choices.why: Right: only the partition column lets days be skipped unopened.

prompt: In `orders.sql`, `dt` appears in no file: Athena reads its value from each object's ___, the `dt=2026-10-01/` written into every one of them.

A crawler runs 200 times in a month, and each run finishes in two minutes on one DPU. Crawls are billed at 0.69 USD per DPU-hour, per second, with a ten-minute minimum for each run. What do the crawls cost for the month, in whole USD?
The Parquet export renames `payment` to `payment_method` from 1 November, and the table is updated to the new name. Read by name, what does a query of `payment_method` return for October?

choices.text: October's payments, as the column is in the same position
choices.why: Parquet is read by name, so position does not carry the values across.

choices.text: An error naming the old column
choices.why: A column a file lacks is not an error when read by name; it is empty.

choices.text: Nothing for October: its files lack the new name
choices.why: Right: a renamed column is lost to every file written before the rename.

choices.text: October's payments, because the catalog version keeps the old name
choices.why: Versions record what the table said; they do nothing to the files.

prompt: A job registers the partition for 1 October with the location `.../orders/dt=2026-10-1/`, one zero short, while the files sit under `dt=2026-10-01/`. What does an Athena query for that day return?

choices.text: No rows, with no error
choices.why: Right: the row names a prefix with nothing in it, and nothing ties the row to the files.

choices.text: The day's rows, as S3 matches prefixes loosely
choices.why: A prefix is an exact string; `dt=2026-10-1/` is not `dt=2026-10-01/`.

choices.text: An `EntityNotFoundException` for the partition
choices.why: The partition exists in the catalog; it is its prefix that is empty.

choices.text: Nothing: `batch-create-partition` refuses a prefix that does not exist
choices.why: The catalog accepted Christmas Day with nothing under it; it checks no prefix.

prompt: One night the export sends a file whose `total_cents` holds text, and next morning every dashboard query on `orders` fails with `HIVE_PARTITION_SCHEMA_MISMATCH`. The nightly crawler was left on its defaults. What happened, and what restores the table?

choices.text: The file corrupted the other 30 days, which have to be rewritten
choices.why: Files are written once; the other days' files did not change.

choices.text: The crawler changed the table; restore its previous version
choices.why: Right: the default, `UPDATE_IN_DATABASE`, writes a disagreeing file's schema into the table.

choices.text: The crawler deleted the table, as its default deletes on change
choices.why: The delete default is to mark a table deprecated when files vanish; nothing vanished.

choices.text: Athena cached the bad file; waiting a day clears it
choices.why: Nothing clears by waiting: the table description itself changed.

The Glue script of the lesson, whose sink adds files, fails after writing 10 of October's 31 days. The bookmark did not move, so the next run reads all 31 raw files again and finishes. What do those 10 days hold now?

choices.text: Each order once, as `dropDuplicates` removes the repeats
choices.why: It removes repeats inside what this run read, not rows already written by the failed run.

choices.text: Each order once, since the bookmark undoes a failed run's writes
choices.why: A bookmark records input; it never removes output.

choices.text: Every order twice, the failed run's files beside the new ones
choices.why: Right: a rerun is safe only if a write replaces its days, as a dynamic partition overwrite does.

choices.text: Nothing: the second run skips days that already have files
choices.why: The script checks no output; the bookmark gave it all 31 inputs.

prompt: In the raw layer, `total_cents` is a number in most files and text in a few. Read into a Glue DynamicFrame, what happens to the column?

choices.text: The read fails on the first file that disagrees
choices.why: That is what a fixed schema has to do; a DynamicFrame does not.

choices.text: The first file's type is used and the others are cast silently
choices.why: That was PyArrow's default in lesson 16, not a DynamicFrame's.

choices.text: Both types are kept until `resolveChoice` settles them
choices.why: Right: each record carries its own schema, which is what DynamicFrames exist for.

choices.text: The column is dropped from every record
choices.why: Nothing is dropped; the disagreement is kept for the script to decide.

prompt: Between two deploys, a developer renames the `transformation_ctx` of the job's `from_catalog` read, with bookmarks on. What does the next run read?

choices.text: Only the files new since the last run, as before
choices.why: The state is kept under the old name, which this read no longer uses.

choices.text: Every raw file again, as no state is kept under the new name
choices.why: Right: the name is the key the bookmark state lives under.

choices.text: Nothing, until the bookmark is reset
choices.why: A missing state means start from the beginning, not stop.

choices.text: The run is refused for an unknown context
choices.why: Any name is accepted; it just has no history.

prompt: `orders` is fully under Lake Formation: `IAM_ALLOWED_PRINCIPALS` is revoked, analysts hold `SELECT` on every column but `phone`, and support holds a tag grant on `internal` and `pii`. Which of these, on AWS, can read phone numbers? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: An analyst querying through Redshift Spectrum

prompt: `orders` is tagged `sensitivity=internal` and `phone` carries `pii`. The pipeline adds a column `email` to the table and gives it no tag. An analyst holds a tag grant on `internal` alone. On AWS, does the analyst read `email`?

choices.text: No: a column with no tag of its own is readable by nobody
choices.why: A column with no tag of its own takes its table's.

choices.text: Yes: tags flow down from the table
choices.why: Right: tags flow down, which is why tagging new columns is a decision about who reads them.

choices.text: Only after a new grant on the table is written
choices.why: That is the per-table grant tags exist to avoid; the existing expression already matches.

choices.text: No: it takes `pii` from the column beside it
choices.why: Tags flow from database to table to column, never sideways.

prompt: A test suite runs against moto and asserts that the analyst's query of the `phone` column is refused. What can it show?

choices.text: That the grants are right, if the test passes

choices.text: Nothing about enforcement: only that the grant requests were well formed
choices.why: Right: even a grant on a table that does not exist is accepted there.

choices.text: That the column is hidden, because moto checks grants on every read
choices.why: The call engines use to be handed credentials answers 404 in moto.

choices.text: That Lake Formation is off, as moto applies the defaults
choices.why: moto applied no default grant to the table at all.

Many questions name a day and some a neighbourhood, so a colleague proposes partitioning the orders by `neighbourhood` and then `dt`, 16 neighbourhoods by 31 days. What does the lesson make of it?

choices.text: A good trade, as every question now opens fewer bytes
choices.why: A question about a month opens every one of the small files, and pays per file.

choices.text: Partition by `dt` and sort by `neighbourhood` inside each file
choices.why: Right: about 500 files a month of some 25 KB each is the small-files failure; sorting gives the statistics something to skip.

choices.text: Fine, because a partition key may have any number of values
choices.why: Every value is at least one file, and a file costs a request and a footer however small.

choices.text: Use `customer_id` instead, as one customer then opens one prefix

prompt: Which of these reduce the bytes read from S3 for `SELECT sum(total_cents) FROM orders WHERE hour >= 21` over the month? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Storing the orders as Parquet rather than CSV
choices.why: Only the two named columns' chunks are read.

choices.text: Writing each file sorted by `hour`, in several row groups
choices.why: The statistics skip the groups whose largest hour is below 21.

choices.text: Compressing the CSV with gzip
choices.why: Every row is still read, and the bytes read are the compressed ones, a fifth here.

choices.text: Shuffling the rows so every group holds every hour
choices.why: Every group then spans 7 to 23 and none is skipped; the shuffled layout read the most of the three.

choices.text: Cutting each day into 96 files
choices.why: The small files read more than the whole layout holds.

prompt: Skipping a row group because its footer's smallest and largest values cannot match a filter is called predicate ___.

At its peak a stream receives 4,500 records a second of 0.5 KB each. A provisioned shard takes 1 MB a second or 1,000 records a second, whichever comes first. What is the smallest number of shards that takes the peak, with no headroom?

A team keys its click stream by the day, `2026-10-16`, so that "a day's clicks stay together", and the stream has ten shards. Writes are throttled every afternoon. What does the lesson say about adding shards?

choices.text: It cures it, since the stream's capacity is the sum of its shards
choices.why: The limit is per shard, and one key hashes to one shard however many there are.

choices.text: It helps only if the new shards are split from the hot one
choices.why: A split divides a range, and a single key's hash is still one point in one of the halves.

choices.text: It does not help: one key hashes to one shard
choices.why: Right: choose the key as the smallest thing whose events must stay in order.

choices.text: It is unnecessary, because on demand would split the key itself
choices.why: On demand adds shards; no mode splits one key across shards.

prompt: Five ordinary consumers each call `GetRecords` on every shard twice a second. What limit of the shard do they meet, and what does the lesson offer for it?

choices.text: The write limit of 1,000 records a second; more shards
choices.why: Reading does not count against the write limit.

choices.text: Its read-call cap, split among them; enhanced fan-out
choices.why: Right: ten calls a second is twice what a shard serves to ordinary consumers.

choices.text: None, as each consumer has its own position in the shard
choices.why: Each has its own position; they still share the shard's read capacity.

choices.text: The retention period, which shortens with every reader
choices.why: Retention does not depend on how many read.

prompt: A consumer that stored the sequence number of the last record it finished resumes just beyond it with a shard iterator of type `___`.

A producer sends Firehose 10 million records a day of 2 KB each, one event per record, for 30 days. Each record is billed rounded up to the next 5 KB, at 0.05800 USD per GB (count 1 GB as 1,000,000 KB). What does ingestion cost for the month, in whole USD?

A delivery stream's prefix is `raw/orders/dt=!{timestamp:yyyy-MM-dd}/`. An order placed in São Paulo (UTC−3) at 22:30 on 15 October 2026 reaches Firehose a second later. On AWS, under which `dt` does it land?

choices.text: `dt=2026-10-15`, the day the customer placed it
choices.why: The expression knows nothing of the order's own date or of São Paulo.

choices.text: `dt=2026-10-16`, because the timestamp is the arrival time in UTC
choices.why: Right: 22:30 in São Paulo is 01:30 UTC the next day.

choices.text: Under the expression as text, `dt=!{timestamp:yyyy-MM-dd}`
choices.why: That is what moto wrote; AWS evaluates the expression.

choices.text: Under the error prefix, as a date expression needs a field from the record
choices.why: That is `partitionKeyFromQuery`; `timestamp` comes from the clock.

prompt: A delivery stream reads the Kinesis stream `orders` as its source. A new service, tested against moto, sends its records to the delivery stream directly with `PutRecordBatch`. What happens on AWS?

choices.text: They are delivered beside the stream's records, as in moto
choices.why: moto accepted the direct put and AWS documents the opposite.

choices.text: Refused: direct puts are not allowed there
choices.why: Right: the service should put its records into `orders` instead.

choices.text: They wait in the Kinesis stream until a shard has room
choices.why: A put to the delivery stream does not travel back into the stream.

choices.text: They are written to the error prefix under `processing-failed`
choices.why: The request is refused at the door; nothing is written anywhere.

prompt: On AWS, which of these records end up under a delivery stream's `ErrorOutputPrefix`? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A record with no `store` field, on a stream partitioned by `partitionKeyFromQuery:store`
choices.why: There is no value to put in the prefix.

choices.text: A record that does not match the Glue table, on a stream converting to Parquet
choices.why: It fails as `format-conversion-failed`.

choices.text: A record the transformation Lambda returned as `ProcessingFailed`
choices.why: It goes under `processing-failed`.

choices.text: A 1 KB record that was billed as 5 KB
choices.why: Rounding changes the bill, not the delivery.

choices.text: A record written in a buffer that the interval flushed half empty
choices.why: A half-empty buffer is delivered as usual, only small.

prompt: A topic on MSK has replication factor 3 and `min.insync.replicas` 2, and one producer is configured with `acks=1`. The leader's broker dies a moment after acknowledging one of that producer's writes. What may have become of the write?

choices.text: Nothing: `min.insync.replicas` 2 guarantees two copies of every write
choices.why: That setting is checked for `acks=all`; with `acks=1` the leader answers alone.

choices.text: It may be lost: only the leader had it
choices.why: Right: a write is as safe as the setting that acknowledged it.

choices.text: It may be refused afterwards, and the producer told to retry
choices.why: The acknowledgement already went out; nothing tells the producer later.

choices.text: It is safe, because MSK replicates between zones for free
choices.why: Free replication is about the bill; the followers may not have fetched it yet.

prompt: `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe` shows a group's three partitions with CURRENT-OFFSET 10, 25 and 7, and LOG-END-OFFSET 14, 25 and 12. How many records is the group behind, in all?
A topic has three partitions, and the team scales the consumer group `lake-copy` to five running members to go faster. What happens?

choices.text: Each partition is split between the members that read it
choices.why: Within a group, a partition has exactly one reader.

choices.text: Every member reads every partition, five times over
choices.why: That is five groups; one group shares the partitions out.

choices.text: The broker refuses the fourth and fifth members
choices.why: They join, and wait for a partition to be handed to them.

choices.text: Three members read one partition each and two sit idle
choices.why: Right: parallelism within a group stops at the partition count.

prompt: A colleague asks MSK for a provisioned cluster of four brokers spread over three Availability Zones. What does the lesson say about that request?

choices.text: It is fine, and the fourth broker goes to the busiest zone
choices.why: MSK places brokers evenly; there is no busiest zone in the request.

choices.text: The broker count must be a multiple of the zones: three or six here
choices.why: Right: brokers are placed evenly across the zones.

choices.text: It is fine, as long as the replication factor is 4
choices.why: The replication factor is per topic; the placement rule is about brokers and zones.

choices.text: moto created such a cluster, so AWS will too
choices.why: moto did not even check that the subnets were real.

prompt: A Kafka consumer uses transactions with `read_committed` and, for each order, charges the customer's card through a payment provider's API. What makes the charge happen once when the consumer crashes and replays?

choices.text: The transaction, which covers the charge as well as the offsets
choices.why: A Kafka transaction stops at Kafka's edge; the provider is outside it.

choices.text: The idempotent producer, which drops the repeated record at the broker
choices.why: That removes a producer's retries; a replay by the consumer reads the same record again.

choices.text: Committing the offset before calling the provider
choices.why: Checkpoint first is at most once: a crash between them loses the charge.

choices.text: Sending the order id as an idempotency key the provider checks
choices.why: Right: the effect lands at the provider, so the dedupe has to be there too.

prompt: A consumer collects whatever arrives in ten seconds into one batch and writes it to S3 under `<shard>/<first seq>-<last seq>.json`, checkpointing after the write. It crashes after a write and before the checkpoint, and replays. What does the lake hold?

choices.text: Each record once, since the key names the content
choices.why: That holds only when a replay cuts the same batches, and a ten-second window does not.

choices.text: Possibly some records twice, under two keys whose ranges overlap
choices.why: Right: the replay reads faster and its window ends elsewhere, so the object is a different one.

choices.text: Nothing new: S3 refuses a second object with the same records
choices.why: S3 compares keys, never contents.

choices.text: A gap: the records of the crashed batch are lost
choices.why: Work first, then the checkpoint, loses nothing.

prompt: The table of processed order ids keeps each item for one day by time to live, and the stream keeps seven days. After a bug, a consumer is pointed back at `TRIM_HORIZON`. What happens to payments from three days ago?

choices.text: They are skipped, as the stream marks what was processed
choices.why: The stream knows nothing of what a consumer did with a record.

choices.text: They are counted again, because their ids have already expired from the table
choices.why: Right: the window must be at least as long as the longest replay anybody would run.

choices.text: They are refused by DynamoDB as too old
choices.why: DynamoDB has no notion of an event's age.

choices.text: They are gone from the stream, so nothing happens
choices.why: Seven days of retention still holds them.

prompt: A consumer writes each of 1,000,000 payments, all items under 1 KB, as a conditional `Put` of its order id and an `Update` of the total, both in one DynamoDB transaction. A transactional write costs twice an ordinary one. How many write units does that take?
A Glue job uses 10 DPUs for 3 hours a night, 30 nights a month, at 0.69 USD per DPU-hour. What does it cost a month, in whole USD?
A team's long-running EMR cluster keeps a lookup table in HDFS, loaded once months ago, and every nightly step reads it. They want to move to a transient cluster each night. What has to change first?

choices.text: Nothing: HDFS survives termination on the core nodes' disks
choices.why: Terminating the cluster deletes HDFS with it.

choices.text: The core nodes have to be Spot, so the table is cheap to keep
choices.why: Spot on core nodes risks the HDFS blocks; it does not keep them.

choices.text: It has to move to S3, outside what is terminated
choices.why: Right: a cluster whose only copy of something is in HDFS can never be stopped.

choices.text: The steps must use `ActionOnFailure=CONTINUE`
choices.why: That decides what follows a failure, not where the data lives.

prompt: An EMR Serverless application is configured with pre-initialised capacity, two drivers and ten workers, so jobs start at once. No job runs all weekend. What did the weekend cost in compute?

choices.text: Nothing, since Serverless bills only the jobs that run
choices.why: Without warm capacity, yes; with it, the capacity is billed while it waits.

choices.text: Everything kept warm, for every hour it waited
choices.why: Right: warm capacity turns Serverless back into something that costs money idle, until auto-stop releases it.

choices.text: A fixed monthly fee per application, whatever it does
choices.why: There is no per-application fee in the lesson's prices.

choices.text: Zero vCPU-hours, as moto's job run showed
choices.why: moto billed nothing for a job that never ran; it says nothing about warm capacity.

prompt: A nightly Spark job of one hour needs a native geospatial library installed on every machine. Which home fits what the lesson weighs?

choices.text: Glue, since it is the cheapest for short, irregular work
choices.why: Glue is the convenient home for short jobs, and on Glue a native library often cannot go at all.

choices.text: A long-running EMR cluster, so the library is installed only once
choices.why: Twenty-three idle hours a night is the most expensive line of the lesson.

choices.text: A transient EMR cluster whose bootstrap action installs it
choices.why: Right: the job needs the machine, and a transient cluster pays only for the night's hours.

choices.text: EMR on EKS, which installs native libraries automatically
choices.why: Nothing installs it for you, and EKS adds a Kubernetes cluster to run.

prompt: In `nightly.json`, somebody removes `.sync` from `LoadOrders`, leaving `arn:aws:states:::glue:startJobRun`. On AWS, what changes about the night's run?

choices.text: Nothing: Step Functions always waits for the job it started
choices.why: Waiting is what `.sync` asks for; without it the state ends when the call returns.

choices.text: The state is refused, as Glue can only be called with `.sync`
choices.why: Starting a job and moving on is a valid integration, and that is the danger.

choices.text: `BuildDaily` may start before the day's orders have finished loading
choices.why: Right: the state moves on as soon as the job is started, not when it succeeds.

choices.text: The retries stop working, but the order of the jobs is kept
choices.why: The order is what breaks: the second job no longer waits for the first.

prompt: An EventBridge Scheduler cron expression such as `cron(0 3 * * ? *)` has ___ fields, the last one for the year, which is why the DAG's `0 3 * * *` is refused on AWS.
Match each part of the Airflow DAG to what plays its part in Step Functions with EventBridge Scheduler.

a timestamp in the execution's input

prompt: Twenty DAGs share one small MWAA environment, which costs 615.02 USD for a month of 730 hours. What does each DAG cost a month, to the nearest whole USD?
A migration keeps a `dms.r6i.large` replication instance (0.56 USD an hour) for 25 days, and then it is deleted. What did the instance cost, in whole USD?

To save effort, a team runs a `full-load` task, not `full-load-and-cdc`, against the live shop database; the copy takes six hours and orders keep arriving. What does the target hold when the task ends?

choices.text: The database exactly as it is at the end of the six hours
choices.why: Nothing after a table's read reaches the target without CDC.

choices.text: Each table as it was when it was read, and none of the changes made since
choices.why: Right: a full load is a copy of each table at its own moment, which is why a live source needs CDC.

choices.text: The database as it was at the start, as DMS freezes the source
choices.why: DMS never stops the source from writing.

choices.text: Nothing, as a full load refuses a source that is being written
choices.why: It runs; the tables just disagree in time.

prompt: The old PostgreSQL sets `max_slot_wal_keep_size`, and a DMS task stays stopped long enough for its slot to fall behind past that size. What happens, by PostgreSQL's documented behaviour?

choices.text: The disk fills, as the setting only warns
choices.why: The setting exists to stop exactly that.

choices.text: The server stops accepting writes until the task resumes
choices.why: The shop keeps writing; it is the slot that is given up.

choices.text: DMS reads the missing log from S3 when it resumes
choices.why: There is no copy of the log for it to read.

choices.text: The server gives up on the slot, and the task has to start again from a new full load
choices.why: Right: the disk is saved at the price of the reader's position.

prompt: Quitanda wants limited LOB mode with `LobMaxSize` 64 for a `notes` column, because it is fast. What does the lesson say to do first?

choices.text: Measure the largest value on the source
choices.why: Right: `SELECT max(octet_length(notes)) FROM orders`, because the failure is silent.

choices.text: Nothing: a longer value fails the task, which then retries in full mode
choices.why: Nothing fails; the value is truncated and the log carries a warning.

choices.text: Run it in moto, which reports truncated values
choices.why: moto stores the settings as text and replicates no row.

choices.text: Turn validation off, as it cannot compare LOBs
choices.why: Validation is the one check that the copy is right; turning it off hides problems.

prompt: A DynamoDB table holds 105 GB. The sheet charges 0.375 USD per GB-month for storage beyond the first 25 GB. What does its storage cost a month, in whole USD?

A new feature keeps each customer's notifications, read by customer newest first, up to 10,000 reads a second at the evening peak, never joined to anything, and deleted after 30 days. Which store does the first question point to?

choices.text: Redshift, which scales by adding nodes
choices.why: A warehouse answers scans in seconds, not one customer's rows in milliseconds.

choices.text: ElastiCache, as the reads must be fast
choices.why: A cache is a copy and may forget; the notifications need a store of record.

choices.text: DynamoDB, keyed by customer and sorted by time, with a time to live
choices.why: Right: one key and a range under it, at any scale, and expiry without a job.

choices.text: Athena over the lake, as the data expires
choices.why: Every read would be a query of seconds, billed at least 10 MB.

prompt: Quitanda's orders could be written to several of these services. Which of them can serve as the store of record for an order? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Aurora PostgreSQL
choices.why: Transactions across the order's tables, kept until deleted.

choices.text: DynamoDB
choices.why: An item stays until something deletes it, and it can carry the order under its keys.

choices.text: ElastiCache
choices.why: It keeps data until eviction or a restart: a copy, never the record.

choices.text: A Kinesis data stream
choices.why: It lets records go after the retention period; it is where events travel.

choices.text: Redshift, loaded from the shop
choices.why: Its keys are declared and not enforced, and it answers as of the last load.

prompt: Finance wants one report a week, over two years of orders already in the lake as Parquet. The team of three runs Aurora and S3 and nothing else. What fits the six questions best?

choices.text: Athena over the lake, paid per query and nothing between them
choices.why: Right: an occasional scan, seconds are fine, and nothing new to operate.

choices.text: A provisioned Redshift cluster, as the data covers two years
choices.why: Billed every hour for a question asked once a week, and one more system to run.

choices.text: Two years of orders loaded into DynamoDB
choices.why: An aggregate over everything is a scan, the pattern DynamoDB is worst at.

choices.text: The query on the Aurora writer, at the evening peak
choices.why: It competes with checkouts, and the history is already in the lake.
